kids.description: Learn chess the fun way! Easy words, big pictures, and lots of gold stars.

lessons.title: 🪖 Meet Your Chess Army!
lessons.content:
Say Hello to Your Team!

Chess is a fun game between two armies — one is White, one is Black. Each army has the SAME pieces. Let's meet them!

🎉 Fun Fact: You get 16 pieces total — 8 pawns and 8 "big pieces". That's a whole team of chess friends!

Your Chess Friends

Who?Looks LikeHow It Moves
👑 King♔ ♚One tiny step, any direction. He's precious — protect him!
👸 Queen♕ ♛Super speedy! Any direction, as far as she likes.
🏰 Rook♖ ♜Straight lines only — up, down, left, right.
⛪ Bishop♗ ♝Diagonal lines only — like sliding on a slanted line.
🐴 Knight♘ ♞Jumps in an "L" shape — 2 steps then 1 turn. It can jump OVER pieces!
🧍 Pawn♙ ♟One step forward (2 steps on its very first move). It captures diagonally!

Setting Up the Board

  • Put a light-colored square at your bottom-right corner. Remember: "light is right!"
  • Pawns line up on the row right in front of you — 8 little soldiers.
  • Rooks go in the corners, then Knights, then Bishops.
  • The Queen always stands on her own color (white Queen on a white square).
  • The King takes the last square.
💡 Grown-Up Tip: Practice setting up the board 3 times in a row without help. Once you can do it fast, you're a real chess player!

lessons.title: 🗺️ Squares Have Names!
lessons.content:
The Board Is Like a Treasure Map

Every square on the chessboard has its very own name, just like every house has an address! This helps us talk about chess moves.

Easy as A-B-C, 1-2-3

  • Going sideways (left to right), the columns are named a, b, c, d, e, f, g, h — just like the alphabet!
  • Going up (bottom to top), the rows are numbered 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8.
  • Every square gets a letter AND a number, like e4 or a1. That's its name!
🎮 Try This Game: Point to a square and say its name out loud. Then close your eyes and try to picture where "d4" is. That's the treasure spot right in the middle!

Why Do We Need Names?

Chess players write down their moves using these names, like a secret code! If someone says "move your Knight to f3", now you know exactly where to go.

The Middle Squares Are Super Important

The four squares in the very center — d4, e4, d5, e5 — are like the castle in the middle of a kingdom. Whoever controls the middle usually has more power!

lessons.title: ✨ Magic Chess Moves!
lessons.content:
Three Super Special Moves

Chess has three "magic moves" that look tricky but are actually easy once you know the secret!

🏰 Castling — Keep Your King Safe!

Castling is a move where your King and Rook team up! The King hops two squares toward the Rook, and the Rook jumps to the other side of the King. It's like your King running into a safe little fort.

Remember: You can only castle if neither piece has moved yet, and nothing is in the way!

👻 En Passant — The Ghost Capture!

Sometimes a pawn tries to sneak past your pawn by jumping two squares at once. You get one special chance to capture it anyway — like catching a ghost before it disappears! But you must do it right away, on your very next move, or the chance vanishes.

👑 Promotion — Pawn Power-Up!

If your little pawn makes it all the way across the board to the last row, something amazing happens: it turns into ANY piece you want (except a King)! Most players choose a Queen because she's the strongest.

🎉 It's like a video game power-up! Your smallest piece becomes your strongest piece.

Two More Rules to Know

  • Checkmate = the King is trapped and can't escape. Game over, you win!
  • Stalemate = the King isn't in danger, but has no safe moves at all. This is a tie — be careful not to do this by accident when you're winning!

lessons.title: 🥷 Sneaky Attacks: Forks & Pins!
lessons.content:
Chess Superpowers!

Great chess players know some sneaky tricks to win pieces. Here are the two easiest superpowers to learn first!

🍴 The Fork Monster

A Fork is when ONE of your pieces attacks TWO enemy pieces at the same time! Your opponent can only save one — you get the other one for free!

🐴 Knights are Fork champions! Their weird L-shaped jump makes them great at forking two pieces at once.

📌 The Unbreakable Pin

A Pin happens when a piece can't move — because if it did, a more important piece behind it (like the King) would be in danger! It's "pinned" in place, like a butterfly on a board (but don't worry, it's safe, just stuck).

⚔️ The Laser Skewer

A Skewer is like a backwards Pin! You attack an important piece first, and when it moves out of the way, you capture the piece hiding behind it. Zap!

🕹️ Practice Time: Before every move, ask yourself: "Can I Fork two pieces? Is anything Pinned? Can I Skewer something?" Superheroes always check for their powers!

lessons.title: 🔍 Checkmate Detective!
lessons.content:
How to Win the Game!

The goal of chess is checkmate — trapping the enemy King so it can never escape. Let's learn the two easiest ways to do it!

👑 + 👸 King and Queen Checkmate

  • Use your Queen to "build a wall" that the enemy King can't cross.
  • Slowly push the enemy King toward the edge of the board — Kings hate corners!
  • Bring your own King closer to help trap the enemy King.
  • Deliver checkmate when the King has nowhere left to run.

👑 + 🏰 King and Rook Checkmate

This one is like a fun dance! Your Rook cuts off a whole row or column, and your King slowly walks over to help push the enemy King to the edge. Then your Rook delivers the final checkmate.

⚠️ Detective Warning: Be super careful not to accidentally trap the enemy King with NO checks and NO safe moves — that's a stalemate, and it's a boring tie instead of a win!

Checkmate Checklist

  • Is the enemy King in check (under attack)?
  • Can the King move to any safe square? If no...
  • Can the King's friends block the attack or capture the attacker? If no...
  • 🎉 That's CHECKMATE! You win!

lessons.title: 🏆 Be a Chess Champion!
lessons.content:
Champions Aren't Just Good at Chess — They're Good Sports!

Being a great chess player isn't only about winning. It's about being kind, patient, and never giving up!

⏰ Meeting the Chess Clock

In real tournaments, each player gets their own clock. Press it after your move so your friend's timer starts. Don't worry — your coach will help the first few times!

✋ Touch-Move Manners

In official games, if you touch a piece on purpose, you have to move it. That's why champions always THINK first, then touch a piece!

📝 Writing Down Your Moves

Just like a detective writes clues in a notebook, chess players write down every move using square names (like "Nf3" for "Knight to f3"). It helps you replay the game later and learn from it!

🤝 Win or Lose, Shake Hands and Smile

  • Say "good game" and shake hands, every single time.
  • If you lose, that's OK! Even world champions lose sometimes.
  • Ask yourself: "What's ONE thing I learned from this game?"
  • Celebrate trying your best — that's what makes a true champion.
🌟 You Did It! Finishing this adventure means you already know more chess than most grown-ups! Time to play your first real game and have fun.

basics.title: Chess Fundamentals
basics.description: Master the essential foundations of chess

lessons.title: The Chess Board & Notation
lessons.content:
Understanding the Board

The chessboard consists of 64 squares arranged in an 8×8 grid. Each square has a unique identifier using algebraic notation.

Files and Ranks

  • Files (columns): Lettered a-h from left to right
  • Ranks (rows): Numbered 1-8 from bottom to top
  • Example: e4 is the square on file e, rank 4
💡 Setup Trick: Always place the board with a light square on your bottom-right corner. Remember: "White on right, queen on her own colour."

Piece Movement Summary

PieceSymbolValueMovement
King♔ ♚∞1 square any direction
Queen♕ ♛9Any distance, any direction
Rook♖ ♜5Horizontal/vertical only
Bishop♗ ♝3Diagonal only
Knight♘ ♞3L-shape (2+1 squares)
Pawn♙ ♟1Forward 1 (or 2 on first move)

lessons.title: Special Rules & Castling
lessons.content:
Special Chess Rules

🏰 Castling

Castling is a special move involving the king and a rook:

  • Kingside (O-O): King moves to g1, rook to f1
  • Queenside (O-O-O): King moves to c1, rook to d1

Conditions: Neither piece has moved, no pieces between them, king not in check, doesn't pass through check.

👻 En Passant

When an enemy pawn advances 2 squares and lands beside your pawn on the 5th rank, you may capture it as if it moved only one square. This right expires after one move!

👑 Pawn Promotion

When a pawn reaches the opponent's back rank, it must promote. Almost always to a Queen, but sometimes to a Knight (for check) or Rook (to avoid stalemate).

🤝 Drawing Rules

  • Stalemate: Not in check but no legal moves = draw
  • Threefold Repetition: Same position occurs 3 times
  • 50-Move Rule: 50 moves without pawn move or capture
  • Insufficient Material: Neither side can force mate

lessons.title: The Three Opening Principles
lessons.content:
Golden Rules for the Opening

1. Control the Centre

Fight for the central squares e4, d4, e5 and d5 with pawns and pieces; do not treat one pawn setup as mandatory. A centre piece controls up to 8 squares; an edge piece controls only 2-3.

Best first moves: 1.e4 or 1.d4 for White

2. Develop Your Pieces

A useful beginner heuristic is to develop efficiently and avoid repeated moves without a concrete reason. Usually develop knights and bishops early.

Goal: Nf3, Nc3, Bc4, castle by move 8-10

3. Ensure King Safety

Castle early to protect your king and connect your rooks. A king in the centre becomes a target.

Aim to castle early when it is safe and useful; move 10 is a guideline, not a rule.
❌ Top 5 Beginner Mistakes:
  1. Bringing queen out too early
  2. Moving same piece twice in opening
  3. Grabbing pawns instead of developing
  4. Not castling
  5. Not checking opponent's threats

lessons.title: Basic Tactical Patterns
lessons.content:
Essential Tactical Motifs

🔱 Fork

A single piece attacks two or more enemy pieces simultaneously. Knights are famous for forks.

White Knight on e5 attacks Black King on g8 and Queen on c7

📌 Pin

A piece cannot move because it would expose a more valuable piece behind it to attack.

White Bishop on g5 pins Black Knight on f6 to the Queen on d8

🔄 Skewer

Similar to a pin, but the more valuable piece is in front. When it moves, the less valuable piece behind is captured.

💥 Discovered Attack

Moving one piece reveals an attack from another piece behind it. Can be devastating!

⚡ Double Attack

One piece creates two threats simultaneously. The opponent can only defend one.

💡 Tactical Thinking: Always look for CHECKS, CAPTURES, and THREATS (CCT) before playing quiet moves.

lessons.title: Advanced Combinations
lessons.content:
Complex Tactical Patterns

🎯 Sacrifice Combinations

Sometimes giving up material leads to a forced win. Common sacrifices:

  • Greek Gift: Bishop sacrifice on h7/h2
  • Smothered Mate: Queen sacrifice to deliver mate with knight
  • Double Bishop Sacrifice: Bxh7+ and Bxg7+

🔗 Clearance Sacrifice

Sacrifice a piece to clear a square, diagonal, or file for a more powerful piece.

🎪 Interference

Place a piece between two enemy pieces to disrupt their coordination.

🧩 Overloading

Force a piece to defend too many targets, then exploit the undefended one.

⚔️ Zwischenzug

"In-between move" - play an unexpected move before taking a captured piece.

lessons.title: Checkmate Patterns
lessons.content:
Essential Checkmate Patterns

🏰 Back Rank Mate

When the king is trapped on the back rank by its own pawns. Very common!

👑 Scholar's Mate

1.e4 e5 2.Bc4 Nc6 3.Qh5 Nf6?? 4.Qxf7# - Learn this to avoid falling for it!

🎯 Smothered Mate

King is checkmated by a knight with no escape squares, surrounded by its own pieces.

🌊 Anastasia's Mate

Knight and rook coordinate to deliver mate on the edge of the board.

⭐ Arabian Mate

Rook and knight deliver mate in the corner. Classic pattern!

🎪 Hook Mate

Rook, knight, and pawn work together to trap the king in a hook shape.

strategy.title: Positional Strategy
strategy.description: Master long-term planning and piece coordination

lessons.title: Pawn Structure Fundamentals
lessons.content:
Understanding Pawn Structures

🏗️ Good vs Bad Pawn Structures

  • Connected Pawns: Pawns on adjacent files supporting each other
  • Passed Pawn: No enemy pawns can stop it from promoting
  • Isolated Pawn: No friendly pawns on adjacent files (weakness)
  • Doubled Pawns: Two pawns on same file (usually weak)
  • Backward Pawn: Cannot be protected by other pawns

🎯 Pawn Breaks

Identify the pawn moves that will open lines for your pieces:

  • Central Break: d4-d5 or e4-e5 to open the centre
  • Wing Break: f4-f5 or b4-b5 to create attacks
💡 Key Principle: "Pawn structure determines the character of the position." - Aaron Nimzowitsch

lessons.title: Piece Activity & Coordination
lessons.content:
Maximizing Piece Power

🎯 Improve Your Worst Piece

Always ask: "Which piece is doing the least?" and improve it first.

🔗 Piece Coordination

  • Bishop Pair: Two bishops are very powerful in open positions
  • Rook on 7th Rank: Dominates and often wins pawns
  • Knight Outpost: A knight on a protected square cannot be attacked by enemy pawns

🎪 Good vs Bad Bishops

Good Bishop: Pawns are on opposite colour squares

Bad Bishop: Pawns are on same colour squares (blocked)

🌟 Open Files & Diagonals

Place rooks on open files, bishops on open diagonals. Control key squares!

lessons.title: Prophylaxis & Prevention
lessons.content:
Thinking Ahead & Preventing Opponent Plans

🛡️ Prophylactic Thinking

Ask: "What does my opponent want to do?" and prevent it!

🎯 Identifying Weaknesses

  • Weak pawns (isolated, backward, doubled)
  • Weak squares (cannot be protected by pawns)
  • Exposed king
  • Uncoordinated pieces

🔧 Fixing Weaknesses

  • Trade pieces when you have structural weaknesses
  • Attack opponent's weaknesses to create counterplay
  • Improve piece placement before launching attacks
💡 Strategic Rule: When you have a structural advantage, trade pieces. When you have a positional disadvantage, keep pieces on the board for tactical chances.

endgames.title: Endgame Essentials
endgames.description: Master the final phase of the game

lessons.title: Basic Checkmates
lessons.content:
Fundamental Checkmate Patterns

👑 King + Queen vs King

Use the queen to cut off the king, then bring your king to help deliver mate. Force the king to the edge.

🏰 King + Rook vs King

Use the rook to cut off the king on a rank/file, then use your king to push the enemy king to the edge.

♟ King + 2 Bishops vs King

Force the king to the corner using the bishops, then deliver mate. Requires coordination!

🐴 King + Bishop + Knight vs King

The most difficult basic checkmate. Force king to corner of your bishop's colour, then use knight to deliver mate.

💡 Endgame Rule: Activate your king! In the endgame, the king becomes a powerful fighting piece.

lessons.title: Pawn Endgames
lessons.content:
King & Pawn Endgames

📏 The Square Rule

To determine if a pawn can queen without support: draw a square from the pawn to the promotion rank. If the enemy king can enter the square, it can catch the pawn.

⚔️ Opposition

When kings face each other with one square between them, the side to move loses the opposition. Use this to outmaneuver the opponent!

🎯 Key Squares

Each pawn has key squares. If your king reaches a key square, the pawn will promote.

🌊 Passed Pawns

  • Outside Passed Pawn: A passed pawn far from other pawns - very valuable
  • Protected Passed Pawn: Supported by another pawn - extremely strong
  • Connected Passed Pawns: Two or more passed pawns together - often decisive

lessons.title: Rook Endgames
lessons.content:
Essential Rook Endgame Knowledge

🏆 Lucena Position

A winning position where the stronger side promotes a pawn. Key technique: "building a bridge" with the rook.

🛡️ Philidor Position

A drawing position where the weaker side holds the draw by keeping the rook on the 6th rank.

🎯 Rook Activity

"Rooks belong behind passed pawns" - whether your own or the opponent's!

📊 Rook + Pawn vs Rook

  • Rook pawns (a/h files) are hardest to promote
  • Central pawns (e/d files) are easiest to promote
  • Active rook can often save drawable positions
💡 Rook Endgame Rule: "All rook endgames are drawn" - but only if you know the drawing techniques!

calculation.title: Calculation & Visualization
calculation.description: Build disciplined thinking: forcing moves, candidate moves, visualization and blunder prevention

lessons.title: CCT Routine
lessons.content:
Checks → Captures → Threats

Before a quiet move, scan forcing moves. Then ask what the opponent changed and what they can capture after your move.

lessons.title: Candidate Moves
lessons.content:
Do not calculate everything

Choose 2–4 serious candidates. Calculate the opponent's strongest reply first, compare final positions, then perform a final blunder check.

lessons.title: Visualization
lessons.content:
Calculate without moving pieces

  • Name the destination square.
  • Visualise the board after your move.
  • Visualise the opponent's best reply.
  • Explain the final position aloud.

competition.title: Tournament & Practical Chess
competition.description: Turn study into reliable over-the-board performance

lessons.title: Tournament Routine
lessons.content:
Before, during and after the game

Arrive calm, use the same opening and thinking routine, spend time at critical moments, and record the game accurately.

lessons.title: Self-Analysis
lessons.content:
Your own thinking first, engine third

  1. Replay the game without an engine.
  2. Mark the critical moment.
  3. Calculate alternatives.
  4. Use a coach or engine to verify.
  5. Write one reusable lesson.

lessons.title: Winning & Defending
lessons.content:
Practical technique

When ahead, reduce unnecessary risk and convert the advantage. When worse, search for active defence, counterplay, perpetual checks or drawing resources.

p1.title: Find the best move for Black
p1.explanation: Playing 1...e5 controls the centre and opens lines for the bishop and queen. This follows the opening principle of controlling the centre.

p2.title: Back-rank mate with bishop cover
p2.explanation: Re8 delivers checkmate along the back rank; the bishop on c3 covers key squares.

p3.title: White to play - complete development
p3.explanation: Castling completes development, brings the king to safety, and connects the rooks. A must-know move!

p4.title: En passant
p4.explanation: The black pawn has just advanced two squares from d7 to d5. White can capture it en passant on d6 immediately.

p5.title: Promotion
p5.explanation: The pawn reaches the last rank and promotes. Queen promotion gives check in this position.

p6.title: Black to play - central reply to 1.d4
p6.explanation: 1...d5 stakes immediate claim in the centre against 1.d4, preventing White from playing e4 easily.

p7.title: White to play - develop knight
p7.explanation: 3.Nc3 develops the knight to its natural square, controls the centre, and prepares for castling.

p8.title: Black to play - castle
p8.explanation: 5...O-O brings the king to safety and connects the rooks. Essential for king safety!

p9.title: White to play - capture loose piece
p9.explanation: dxe4 captures the unprotected black knight on e4, winning material and strengthening the centre.

p10.title: Knight fork — king and rook
p10.explanation: Nc7+ forks the king on e8 and the rook on a8, winning a full rook on the next move.

p11.title: White to play - pin
p11.explanation: Bg5 pins the knight on f6 to the queen on d8. The knight cannot move without losing the queen.

p12.title: Rook & king back rank mate
p12.explanation: Re8 delivers checkmate because the white king on f6 prevents the black king from stepping to g7.

p13.title: White to play - prepare central break
p13.explanation: c3 prepares the powerful d4 pawn break to challenge Black in the centre.

p14.title: White to play - double attack
p14.explanation: Ng5 attacks both the f7 pawn and the bishop on g4. Black cannot defend both.

p15.title: White to play - strike at f7
p15.explanation: Bxf7+ sacrifices the bishop to expose Black's king and shatter king safety.

p16.title: White to play - Fried Liver setup
p16.explanation: Ng5 creates dual threats against the vulnerable f7 square.

p17.title: Knight fork — winning the rook
p17.explanation: Nc7+ forks the king on e8 and the corner rook on a8, winning decisive material.

p18.title: Black to play - exploit overloaded queen
p18.explanation: The white queen is overloaded defending multiple points. Exploiting this wins material.

p19.title: White to play - central pawn break
p19.explanation: Playing d4 immediately strikes at Black's central pawn on e5.

p20.title: White to play - back rank mate
p20.explanation: Re8# delivers checkmate on the back rank. The king is trapped by its own pawns.

p21.title: Queen & king mate in one
p21.explanation: Qg7# delivers checkmate supported by the king on g6. The cornered king has no legal moves.

p22.title: Back rank mate with knight escort
p22.explanation: The rook mates along the back rank while the knight controls escape squares.

p23.title: Two rooks lawnmower checkmate
p23.explanation: Rb8# completes the lawnmower ladder mate, cutting off the final rank from the king.

p24.title: Rook mate with knight clamp
p24.explanation: The rook delivers a back-rank mate; the knight covers key escape squares.

p25.title: White to play - exploit isolated pawn
p25.explanation: c4 puts pressure on the centre and fixes the pawn structure.

p26.title: Centralise the king to support passed pawn
p26.explanation: Bring the king toward the centre and ahead of the pawn to establish key squares.

p27.title: Rook on 7th rank to checkmate
p27.explanation: Ra8# delivers checkmate on the rim with king support on f6.

p28.title: White to play - solid development
p28.explanation: d3 solidifies the central e4 pawn and frees the c1 bishop.

p29.title: White to play - prophylactic move
p29.explanation: h3 prevents ...Bg4 and creates a luft (escape square) for the king.

p30.title: White to play - flank clamp
p30.explanation: a4 prevents Black's queenside expansion with ...b5.

p31.title: Rook edge checkmate
p31.explanation: Ra7# delivers checkmate against the cornered king with king support on b6.

p32.title: Rook mate in one
p32.explanation: The rook on f8 checks the king on h8; the king cannot escape because the white king controls g7.

p33.title: Win the rook
p33.explanation: The bishop captures the exposed rook on h7. Always scan diagonals for loose pieces.

p34.title: White to play - square rule sprint
p34.explanation: The pawn can queen because the black king cannot enter the square (h5-h8-d5-d8).

p35.title: King opposition in endgame
p35.explanation: Kd3 takes the direct opposition against the black king, controlling the path for the d-pawn.

p36.title: King and pawn support
p36.explanation: Keep the king close to the pawn and improve its support.

p37.title: Lucena practice
p37.explanation: Start the Lucena technique by placing the rook on the eighth rank.

p38.title: Rook check on back rank
p38.explanation: Keep the rook active and check from the back rank.

p39.title: Trade into winning King & Pawn ending
p39.explanation: Rxd6 captures the black rook, simplifying into an easily won endgame.

x1.title: Scholar's mate pattern attack
x1.explanation: Qxf7# delivers checkmate because the queen on f7 is defended by the bishop on c4 and the black king has no legal squares.

x2.title: Rook & king edge checkmate
x2.explanation: Ra8# delivers checkmate along the 8th rank. The white king on d6 blocks the black king from stepping to d7, e7, or c7.

x3.title: Back-rank mate
x3.explanation: The rook reaches e8 and mates because the king is boxed in by its own pawns.

x4.title: Rook and knight coordination
x4.explanation: The rook gives the final back-rank check while the knight helps control escape squares.

x5.title: Knight centralisation
x5.explanation: Centralise the knight and practise looking for future fork squares rather than moving automatically.

x6.title: Rook cut-off in endgame
x6.explanation: Rd7 cuts the black king off along the 7th rank, trapping it on the edge of the board.

x7.title: Back-rank mate with rook
x7.explanation: The rook mates along the back rank because the king is boxed in by its own pawns.

x8.title: Queen back-rank checkmate
x8.explanation: Qe8# delivers checkmate along the back rank with the queen.

x9.title: Find the winning king move
x9.explanation: King placement decides pawn endings. Take the opposition before pushing the pawn.

x10.title: Push with king support
x10.explanation: Bring the king toward the pawn before rushing the pawn forward.

x11.title: King in front of pawn
x11.explanation: Centralise the king so it can support the pawn and control promotion squares.

x12.title: King opposition defense & breakthrough
x12.explanation: Maintain control over the key squares in this king and pawn endgame.

x13.title: Passed pawn support
x13.explanation: King activity is often more important than an automatic pawn push.

x14.title: Opposition before promotion
x14.explanation: Use king positioning and opposition rather than pushing the pawn blindly.

x15.title: Rook check from behind
x15.explanation: An active rook can check from behind while the king approaches.

x16.title: Direct opposition in King & Pawn ending
x16.explanation: Kd6 takes key square control and outflanks Black's king, guaranteeing pawn promotion.

x17.title: Back-rank rook check
x17.explanation: The rook reaches the back rank and mates the boxed king.

x18.title: Do not stalemate — queen mate in one
x18.explanation: Qf8# delivers checkmate without allowing stalemate.

x19.title: Queen check
x19.explanation: A long-range queen check demonstrates how diagonals can create forcing moves.

x20.title: Rook activity
x20.explanation: An active rook check can restrict the enemy king; always examine the king’s replies.

x21.title: Bishop skewer on king and rook
x21.explanation: The bishop captures the undefended rook on h8, winning decisive material.

x22.title: Knight fork on pawn & king square
x22.explanation: Nf4 increases knight activity, hitting the weak e6 pawn.

x23.title: Queen check
x23.explanation: Combine checking ability with restriction, while counting the opponent’s legal replies.

x24.title: Active rook check
x24.explanation: An active rook can check from behind and restrict the king.

y1.title: Win the rook with knight fork/capture
y1.explanation: The knight captures the loose rook; scan for valuable targets on knight moves.

y2.title: Capture the pinned knight
y2.explanation: The bishop removes the pinned knight and gives check.

y3.title: Capture the skewer target
y3.explanation: The rook captures the exposed rook and continues the check along the file.

y4.title: Back-rank conversion with knight guard
y4.explanation: Re8 pins and attacks the black rook on f8, threatening immediate mate.

y5.title: Forcing queen check
y5.explanation: A forcing queen check makes the opponent respond immediately.

y6.title: Rook pin on queen & king
y6.explanation: The rook captures the pinned queen with check, winning the queen for a rook.

y7.title: Rook on 7th rank pressure
y7.explanation: Ra8 puts maximum back-rank pressure on the pinned rook on f8.

y8.title: Promote safely to queen
y8.explanation: Promote the pawn on g7 to a queen, creating a winning advantage.

y9.title: King opposition defense
y9.explanation: Kd1 maintains king opposition and prepares to defend the e2 pawn.

y10.title: Opposition and pawn advance
y10.explanation: Step toward the centre and take the opposition before pushing the pawn.

y11.title: Support the passed pawn
y11.explanation: Bring the king into the action to support the d-pawn's advance.

y12.title: Cut off the king with rook check
y12.explanation: A rook check on d2 forces the king backward and controls the d-file.

y13.title: Rook behind the king — back rank mate
y13.explanation: Check from the a-file rook delivers back-rank checkmate.

y14.title: Bishop activity on diagonal
y14.explanation: Place the bishop on an active diagonal and improve its reach.

y15.title: Knight fork setup
y15.explanation: A central knight creates a forcing check on e7.

y16.title: Rook check on open file
y16.explanation: Use the open file to give a forcing check.

y17.title: Bishop capture with check
y17.explanation: Move the bishop to h7 to capture the h-pawn and create a forcing check on the king.

y18.title: Queen activity — back rank mate
y18.explanation: The queen reaches e8 and delivers a back-rank mate.

y19.title: Rook clamp on back rank
y19.explanation: Re8# mates the boxed king on the back rank.

y20.title: Rook mate in one
y20.explanation: A classic back-rank mate along the e-file to e8.

z1.title: Knight fork — queen and rook
z1.explanation: Nc6 attacks both the queen on b8 and the rook on d8 at the same time. Black can only save one piece — always scan knight moves for double attacks.

z2.title: Bishop fork — two rooks
z2.explanation: Bd5 sits on the diagonal that touches both a8 and g8 at once. A well-placed bishop can fork just as effectively as a knight.

z3.title: Queen fork — rank and file
z3.explanation: Qd5 attacks the rook on a5 along the 5th rank and the rook on d8 along the d-file simultaneously — the queen can fork using any of its lines at once.

z4.title: Discovered check with a capture
z4.explanation: The knight was blocking the rook on e1. Nxd7 captures a piece and simultaneously opens the e-file, giving check from the rook — a discovered check that also wins material.

z5.title: Double check
z5.explanation: Nd6+ is a double check: the knight itself attacks e8, and moving it off the e-file reveals a check from the rook on e1. On a double check the only legal reply is to move the king — no block or capture can answer both checks.

z6.title: Smothered mate finish
z6.explanation: The black king on h8 is boxed in by its own rook and pawns. Nf7 delivers checkmate because the king has no flight square and nothing can capture or block a knight check.

z7.title: Anastasia's mate
z7.explanation: The knight on e7 covers g8, the black pawn on g7 blocks the other escape square, and Rh1 checks all the way down the open h-file with no flight square left — a textbook Anastasia’s mate.

z8.title: Boxed king — bishop mate
z8.explanation: Black’s own rook and bishop block every flight square around the king, and the pawns on b7/c7 cannot interpose. Be6 delivers mate along the long diagonal — a reminder that a boxed-in king is often more dangerous than a centralised one.

z9.title: Count the attackers and defenders
z9.explanation: The pawn on d5 looks defended by the queen, but a second white attacker — the pawn on c4 — also guards d5. If Black recaptures with the queen, cxd5 wins the queen for a knight and a pawn. Always count every attacker and defender of a square before assuming a piece is safe.

z10.title: Underpromotion fork
z10.explanation: Promoting to a queen or rook allows Black to play ...Rxa7 or creates an escape, but promoting to a knight gives check to the king and forks the rook on a7 simultaneously — an underpromotion tactic where a knight achieves what a queen cannot.

m1.title: Discovered attack on the queen
m1.explanation: Qe2 pins the e4 knight against the black queen, preparing to win material with d3 and discovered check.

m2.title: Knight outpost jump
m2.explanation: Qd2 challenges the active black queen and prepares to centralise White's rooks on the d-file.

m3.title: Deflection of the bishop
m3.explanation: h3 asks the bishop what it wants to do, forcing it to retreat or trade on f3 without damaging pawn structure.

m4.title: Quiet prophylactic move
m4.explanation: h3 prevents ...Bg4 pin and creates a secure escape square on h2 for the king in the middlegame.

m5.title: Central tension release
m5.explanation: Castling secures the king before resolving the central pawn tension on e4 and d5.

m6.title: Bishop attack with tempo
m6.explanation: Be3 develops the dark-squared bishop with tempo, attacking the overextended black queen on c5.

m7.title: Back-rank mate in the endgame
m7.explanation: Re8# delivers checkmate despite Black being up a full queen! Never neglect back-rank safety.

m8.title: Sicilian central breakthrough
m8.explanation: 12.e5! strikes at the center, attacking the f6 knight and unmasking a kingside attacking storm.

m9.title: Yugoslav Attack king safety preparation
m9.explanation: Qd2 prepares O-O-O and the Bh6 trade in the Dragon Sicilian.

m10.title: The c-file knight jump tactic
m10.explanation: Nd5! is the thematic Sicilian tactical strike exploiting the pinned c7 queen along the c-file.

m11.title: Pawn center classical clamp
m11.explanation: e4 creates a powerful classical central pawn duo in the Queen's Gambit.

m12.title: Connecting rooks in the opening
m12.explanation: Qc2 connects the rooks and controls the critical c-file and e4 square.

m13.title: Break the pin with castling
m13.explanation: Castling breaks the absolute pin on the knight and brings the king to safety.

m14.title: Endgame back-rank mate down open file
m14.explanation: Rd8# delivers instant checkmate down the open d-file against the boxed king.

m15.title: Rook capture with checkmate
m15.explanation: Rxd8# captures the rook and delivers back-rank checkmate.

m16.title: Break the pin with castling king
m16.explanation: Castling completes development and unpins the c3 knight.

m17.title: London System castle
m17.explanation: Castles completes the London System pyramid setup safely.

m18.title: Save the queen from bishop attack
m18.explanation: Qd8 retreats the attacked queen to a safe central coordination square.

m19.title: King advance in pawn ending
m19.explanation: Ke5 seizes the opposition and outflanks the black king.

m20.title: Pawn advance on key squares
m20.explanation: Kd5 controls the key promotion squares in front of the e6 pawn.

g20.annotation: Fischer converts a 4-vs-3 queenside pawn majority with dominant rook invasion on the 7th rank, forcing Petrosian's capitulation.

gx1.annotation: A beginner-friendly opening drill: defend f7, develop pieces, and castle instead of chasing the queen.

gx2.annotation: Use this mini-game to pause before every capture and ask what pieces become loose after the exchange.

gx3.annotation: Do not race the pawn automatically. King position and opposition decide the result.

gx4.annotation: The attacking rook cuts off the king while the friendly king approaches. This is a practical model, not a memorised sequence.

gx5.annotation: Before every move, name all checks you can see. Then ask whether the check actually improves the position.

gx6.annotation: A quiet development game. Pause after every move and identify which pieces are attacked and defended.

gx7.annotation: A model mini-game for development, centre control and king safety. Pause after every move and ask what changed.

gx8.moves: 1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 dxe4 4.Nxe4 Bf5 5.Ng3 Bg6 6.Nf3 Nd7
gx8.annotation: Use this as a repertoire rehearsal: identify the purpose of each developing move instead of memorising the sequence.

gx9.moves: 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 a6 4.Bxc6 dxc6 5.O-O Bd6 6.d4 exd4 7.Qxd4
gx9.annotation: Practise evaluating a queen trade and the resulting pawn structure rather than automatically avoiding exchanges.

gx10.annotation: The objective is not to win quickly. Notice how development and castling make the position easier to play.

gx11.annotation: A simple transition into a king-and-pawn ending. Ask whose king is more active and why.

gx12.annotation: After each move, name the opponent’s threat before choosing your next move.

gg1.annotation: Wijk aan Zee, 1999, round 4. Kasparov sacrifices a rook on move 24 and then a second exchange, dragging the black king from a7 all the way to d1 in a forced sequence. Topalov resigned on move 44 facing an unstoppable mating attack. Widely rated among the greatest games ever played.

gg2.annotation: New York, 11 May 1997, the deciding sixth game of the historic rematch. Deep Blue’s piece sacrifice 8.Nxe6 shattered Black’s position, and Kasparov resigned after only 19 moves — the first time a reigning World Champion lost a match to a computer.

gg3.annotation: Tilburg, 1991. After winning total control of the position, Short marches his own king up the board — Kh2-g3-f4-g5 — to help deliver mate while Black's queen and rooks can do nothing about it. Timman resigned facing unstoppable mate. A famous demonstration that king safety rules can be broken once the position allows it.

gg4.annotation: Berlin, 1852. Anderssen's other true masterpiece besides the Immortal Game. The point is the astonishing 19.Rad1!, offering both rooks and setting up a forced mate — culminating in a queen sacrifice, 21.Qxd7+!!, that finishes the game with three quiet-looking bishop moves.

gg5.opening: The Game of the Decade (King's Indian / Grünfeld)

gg6.annotation: Candidates Match 1965. Tal unloads a hurricane of dynamic sacrifices on the kingside (26.Nxh6! and 33.Re8!), demonstrating the supreme power of initiative over material balance.

gg9.annotation: World Championship 1972, Game 6. Fischer surprises Spassky with 1.c4 (having never played it in serious matchplay) and produces an artistic masterpiece. Spassky famously joined the audience in applauding Fischer at the end.

gg12.annotation: World Championship 2013, Game 9. Anand launches a desperate kingside counter-thrust, but Carlsen calculates all defensive resources with icy precision, pushing his passed pawns on e6 and d6 to seal his first World Championship title.
